narrator.instruct: Gripping, energetic storyteller telling a true Cold War thriller, brisk and tense, never calm.

officer.instruct: A young Soviet duty officer in a bunker, panicked and urgent, almost shouting over an alarm.

petrov.instruct: A calm, firm military officer under huge pressure, steady and decisive, quietly certain.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: In nineteen eighty-three, a computer told one Soviet officer that American missiles were coming. He decided the computer was wrong.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: September twenty-sixth, just after midnight. A secret bunker outside Moscow.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Lieutenant Colonel Stanislav Petrov is on watch. Weeks earlier, Soviet jets shot down a Korean airliner. Moscow fears an American first strike.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then the siren. One American missile, launched. Then another. Then five.

lines.speaker: officer
lines.text: Comrade Petrov! What do we report?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: His job: pass it up the chain. Moscow would have minutes to decide.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You see, a real first strike wouldn't be five missiles. It would be hundreds.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: And ground radar had nothing to confirm yet.

lines.speaker: petrov
lines.text: False alarm. Report a system fault.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The satellite had mistaken sunlight glinting off high clouds for rocket fire.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now, what if he'd reported an attack? His warning would have climbed to the Kremlin.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Would they have fired? Some say other checks would have stopped it. Nobody wants to find out.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: His reward? No medal back then. A reprimand, he said, over paperwork. The story stayed secret for fifteen years.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Petrov later called it fifty-fifty. He bet the computer was wrong. And he was right.
